No classroom example doubles twice per step like tile pyramids — counts make exponential growth visceral.

Cumulative world tiles through z12 ≈ 22.4 million — storable. Through z15 ≈ 1.43 billion — a data centre's opinion changes. Each single zoom from z13 up exceeds all previous zooms combined, three times over.
A city needs only its rectangle of the grid — thousands to millions of tiles, not billions. Counts by region (width × height in tiles, summed over zooms) are the practical form of this page's math.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
The number of tiles in the full grid at a zoom (2^z × 2^z = 4^z) and, for regions, the rectangle counts per zoom summed across the pyramid.
Which map standard does it use?
The slippy-map standard (Web Mercator, 256-px tiles) shared by OSM, Google and MapLibre.
Can I use this in production GIS?
The formulas are the production standard itself — yes for web-mapping work.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 — tile systems are defined over it.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — tiles and pixels quantise; decimals beyond the cell are decoration.
Why does nobody pre-render everything?
This table. Rendering and storage grow ×4 per zoom while demand concentrates on a sliver of tiles — on-demand rendering with caching wins by orders of magnitude.
Vector tiles change the count?
The grid is identical; tile sizes differ (often smaller, style-dependent). Counts govern both.
How many tiles for my city?
Rectangle math: (x_east − x_west + 1) × (y_south − y_north + 1) per zoom — corner tiles from the tile calculator, summed over your zoom range.
Ocean tiles really stored?
Smart stacks skip or placeholder them (a single ocean tile serves all seas in some systems) — the count is the naive ceiling, engineering is the discount.
Tile size assumption?
~15 KB is a planning average for raster map tiles; satellite imagery runs far larger, sparse vector tiles far smaller. State your assumption when budgeting.
